replacement: r [ Massachusetts law also made adultery punishable by death, and Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 441, says that several people were in fact executed for it. He tells a curious story from the year 1663. A married woman had had an adulterous relationship with a young man. Her husband died, and she married her lover. Several years went by before people began to suspect the couple’s earlier adulterous relationship. They were thrown into prison and brought to trial, and they very narrowly escaped the death penalty.]

replacement: In this body of penal laws, the legislators cared above all about keeping the community orderly and moral. They invaded the realm of conscience again and again, and there was hardly a sin that the magistrates could not censure. The reader has seen how rigorously these laws punished rape and adultery. Sex between unmarried people was also harshly suppressed. The judge had the power to impose a fine, a whipping, or marriage *s on offenders, and if the records of the old courts of New Haven can be believed, such prosecutions were not uncommon. One sentence, dated the first of May, 1660, fines and reprimands a young woman who was accused of using improper language and letting herself be kissed. *t The Code of 1650 is full of preventive measures. It deals severely with idleness and drunkenness. *u Innkeepers may not serve any customer more than a fixed amount of liquor, and plain lying, whenever it may do harm, *v is checked with a fine or a flogging. Elsewhere the legislator completely forgets the great principles of religious toleration that he himself had defended in Europe. He makes attendance at divine service compulsory, *w and he even goes so far as to inflict severe punishment, ** and even death, on Christians who chose to worship God according to a ritual different from his own. *x At times the zeal of his enactments leads him down to the pettiest details; the same Code, for instance, contains a law that forbids the use of tobacco. *y We must not forget that these fantastical and vexatious laws were not imposed from above. All the people concerned voted for them freely, and the customs of the community were even more austere and puritanical than the laws. In 1649 a solemn association was formed in Boston to put a stop to the worldly luxury of long hair. *z
